transcript.reader:
Let me check I have your case, so I test the right thing. You're saying the real content hidden behind the Church-Turing hypothesis is a physical claim — every finitely realizable physical system can be perfectly simulated by a universal model computing machine working by finite means — and that quantum theory, through the universal quantum computer Q, meets this claim where classical physics and the Turing machine cannot. Is that a fair version, and is the thing you're explaining *why* quantum theory is compatible with (1.2), or *whether* (1.2) is true of Nature?

Two questions to start. First: which is on the hook — that quantum theory is *compatible* with (1.2), or that (1.2) actually holds in the world? Second: what is the other thing that could have happened? If the world had been one where Q could *not* simulate some finite physical system, what would we have seen instead, and where would we have looked?
transcript.author:
Fair version, with one distinction I must insist on. What I *demonstrate* is compatibility: quantum theory does not contradict (1.2), because Q perfectly simulates any system with a finite-dimensional state space — a dense subset of superscattering matrices, closed under convex combination, covers it. Whether (1.2) actually holds in Nature I explicitly leave open: it "must remain open until the state space and dynamics of the universe are understood better." So the conditional claim is on the hook; the cosmological one is an empirical conjecture, weakly corroborated by the Bekenstein bound if black-hole thermodynamics is trustworthy.

The other way it could have gone: some finitely realizable system whose dynamics are *not* the projection of unitary evolution in a larger space — i.e., not of the superscattering form (3.8)–(3.10) — or with no finite bound on distinguishable states. We would have looked exactly where I looked: at whether the physically realizable set G is really an open set in J, which is what my argument from irreversibility and the third law (1.3) supplies. If a finite process could produce pure states, the strictly unitary case (3.13) would be realizable, and the entropy argument collapses.

Experimentally, we look by testing the linearity of quantum dynamics, which I list as a Q-program worth writing. And note the dependence: (1.2) holds only on the assumption that (1.3) is true.

transcript.reader:
Good — compatibility, not cosmology. Now let me take it apart in your own words. I'd list the parts doing the work as: (a) perfect simulation, defined as a black-box functional match under labellings; (b) Q's "finite means" conditions (i)–(iii); (c) the third law (1.3), read as "no finite process drives entropy or temperature to zero"; (d) your claim that no realizable system can be prepared in a pure, uncorrelated state; (e) density matrices, with the superscattering matrix $ as the general dynamics; (f) the step that the physically realizable set G is open in J; (g) the dense-subset-plus-convex-combination finish. Is that a fair version of your case, and which of those parts, if any, is doing no work?

Second: what is on your change list? You've drawn the range at finite-dimensional state spaces and put superselection sectors outside it — was that limit fixed before you looked or after? Give me the neighbouring limit I could swap it for, and tell me what should break: where would we see that the line has been drawn in the wrong place?
transcript.author:
Largely fair, with an honest admission. (a) does work: it fixes the standard of success, and by making it a functional black-box match it avoids triviality. (b) does work only as a constraint, not as a discriminator — both T and Q satisfy (i)–(iii); it excludes cheating, not classicality. (c) and (d): these are nearly the same assertion. (d) is what actually drives the argument; (c) is the label I hang on it. One of them is doing no independent work — I'd say (c), since (d) is the operative premise. (e) is partly display: the superscattering index structure is more machinery than the proof needs. What the argument requires of the general dynamics is only that the realizable set be convex and non-extremal — that it contains mixtures and not just the unitary points. (f) and (g) do the real work: openness is what converts "countably dense subset" into "every state." So the load-bearing parts are (a), (d), (f), (g); (e) is formalism carrying (d).

Second: the finite-dimensional restriction was drawn *after*, and I should say so plainly. I derived it where I had a proof — a finite state space makes the convex-combination finish go through — not because I have an argument that Nature is finite. The Bekenstein bound is the only independent support, and it's conditional on black-hole thermodynamics.

The neighbouring limit: infinite-dimensional state space, the realm of quantum field theory. What should break is exact perfect simulation: with unbounded distinguishable states, no finite-memory-per-step unitary reproduces the system exactly; I could promise only approximation, which is precisely what I refused to call perfect simulation of classical systems. The other swap is my exclusion of superselection sectors. If I drew that line wrongly, we'd see it in a system whose realizable set isn't open — and most sharply in black-hole evaporation, if information loss is genuine, giving non-unitary dynamics not of the form (3.8).

transcript.reader:
Two pokes. Take (d) — no realizable system can be prepared in a pure, uncorrelated state. Give me one change to the world your argument says *would* alter whether (d) holds, and one it says *would not*. And if (d) were false — if some finite process could prepare a pure state — walk me through where the proof actually breaks: does the realizable set G stop being open, or does the dense-subset-plus-convex-combination finish survive with one extra step?

Second: you say (c) is just the label you hang on (d). Is the openness of G the same way — (d) under another name in the geometry of density matrices — or does the geometry do independent work? Put it as a test: is there any step between (d) and "every finite system is perfectly simulated" that could fail *even with (d) granted*? If not, I have to ask whether the answer was in the starting points all along.
transcript.author:
**On (d).** One change that would alter it: a false third law. If a finite process could drive the correlation degrees of freedom to zero temperature, pure uncorrelated states become preparable and (d) fails outright. That is the only lever. One that would not: enlarging the heat bath, altering its Hamiltonian, or changing the coupling strength. Any non-zero coupling leaves the system mixed; (d) is robust to those details. (Superselection is a third case: excluding it changes the left inequality of (3.12), not (d).)

If (d) were false: G stops being open. It would then include its extremal points — the strictly unitary superscattering matrices (3.13). Convex combinations of a dense subset still fill the interior, but no finite convex combination of interior points lands on a boundary point. So the (g) finish fails exactly on the boundary, and only strictly dissipative systems get *perfect* simulation; ideal closed systems get approximation, which is what I refused to call perfect for classical systems. So it is not one extra step — the theorem's target shrinks.

**On openness.** No, openness is not (d) renamed; the geometry does independent work. (d) says the preparable *states* avoid the boundary. (f) says the realizable *dynamics* form an open set in J. Grant (d) completely and the couplings in the universe might still be restricted to a discrete, measure-zero set — then G has empty interior and the convex-combination trick has no open region to work in. The missing premise is that arbitrary couplings actually occur, i.e. no superselection.

And the strongest test: §2's universality theorem. (d) says nothing about whether eight generators on one bit compose to a group dense in the unitary group. I had to construct that by induction. That burden is genuinely independent — otherwise the paper would be a tautology.

transcript.reader:
Two things, both pokes.

First, the (d)/(1.3) lever. You say (1.3) cannot be directly refuted — no finite-accuracy measurement tells absolute zero from an arbitrarily small positive temperature. But you've just told me the *only* thing that could make (d) fail is a false third law. So what change to the world could we actually make that would show (d) is false? If none, then is (d) held by anything we could check, or is it a requirement you set — fixed rather than fitted?

Second, reverse on Everett. Had the many-worlds reading been wrong and a conventional interpretation right, would any prediction in your compatibility theorem change — any state, any probability, any running time? If nothing would change, then the claim that the other interpretations place "an intolerable strain" is held by a different explanation that is not being tested here, and I should mark it borrowed, not held. Name the change that would tell the two apart, and tell me where we would read it off.
transcript.author:
**On (d).** You've caught me. No experiment I can name would show (d) false. Reaching zero entropy by finite means is impossible precisely *because* no finite-accuracy measurement discriminates — so the very statement that makes (d) falsifiable is unobservable. Concede: (d) is fixed, not fitted. I set it as a requirement, via (1.3). The paper's own structure admits this: I say (1.2) is corroborated only "indirectly," and I even mused that (1.3) might be *derived* from (1.2) plus quantum theory — which, if it worked, would demote (d) from axiom to theorem. As written, it is an assumption, not a result. The nearest thing to a check is dynamical, not thermometric: genuine information loss in black-hole evaporation would signal non-unitary, non-(3.8) dynamics, and that is where (d) would break. But that is a search, not a finite-accuracy test. So yes — held, not fitted.

**On Everett.** Nothing changes. States, probabilities, running times, the superscattering structure, the openness argument — identical under Everett or Copenhagen, because the theorem is about the formalism, and the formalism is shared. So the "intolerable strain" line is not carried by anything here; it rests on a separate explanatory argument, and on the experiment in Deutsch (1985). Mark it borrowed, not held. The change that would tell them apart: whether dynamics are linear at all scales. If the conventional reading is right and collapse is real, unitarity fails somewhere; Everett requires it never to. Where we'd read it off: the linearity test I listed, Bell-inequality tests, and the self-measurement experiment — all needing quantum computers, which is why the test is deferred and the strain-claim stays explanatory for now.

transcript.reader:
Let me source two parts and then build a rival.

(i) The §3 running-time bound, N² − 2N + 2 times τ: you say you could not construct examples for N > 2 and you put it forward as a conjecture. Is that fitted, built or asserted — and what case would settle it? (ii) The Bekenstein bound (3.15) is the only thing keeping the cosmological form of (1.2) alive, and it comes with "if the theory of the thermodynamics of black holes is trustworthy." Which mark does it get?

Now the rival. Build the strongest one properly: a classical stochastic theory with genuine randomness. By (3.1)–(3.6) and Bell (1964) it cannot reproduce Q's joint correlations, though it can get arbitrarily close to any single-bit probability. Name the one change that separates the two and where we read it off. Then tell me whether your compatibility argument turns on what comes *out* or on how it *works* — could a quite differently built machine give the same finite-dimensional statistics, and would that satisfy (1.2) just as well?
transcript.author:
(i) **Asserted.** It's a conjecture, not fitted or built: I attained the N=2 bound and could construct nothing beating N²−2N+2 for N>2, so I guessed it optimal. Settled by any one of three things — an explicit decoding program achieving that mean time, a single N>2 example beating it (which refutes), or a proof of the lower bound from unitarity in the style of (3.19)–(3.20).

(ii) **Borrowed.** It comes with a conditional — "if the theory of the thermodynamics of black holes is trustworthy" — and carries no independent weight here. Granted that, it bounds N(A).

**Rival.** The classical stochastic machine matches every single-bit probability (3.2); it cannot match Q's joint correlations. The separating change is locality/non-separability: a classical stochastic theory is local and must obey Bell's inequality; the state (3.3) and the consecutive measurements at (3.5) and (3.6) violate it. Read off there, in the joint statistics — not the marginals. It gets arbitrarily close to each bit alone, never to the pair.

**What comes out, not how it works.** Perfect simulation is defined behaviourally, by a black-box functional match under labellings. So a quite differently built machine yielding the same superscattering matrix satisfies (1.2) just as well. Structure mattered only in §2, where I had to *prove* Q universal; the principle itself asks for output statistics, not for my particular hardware.

transcript.reader:
Two last pokes, then I'm done asking.

First, the patches. The finite-dimensional restriction was drawn *after*, and the reason you gave is a fact about you — there was a proof there — not a fact about Nature. Swap that limit for the infinite-dimensional neighbour and something breaks, but nothing *inside* your explanation says why things differ outside the line. So does your explanation itself hold that limit, or does it just state it? Same question for the superselection exclusion — "a possibility that we lose no generality by excluding." Is that a patch made in advance? If so, what would we measure to show it is swallowing a job rather than doing one — what reading would worry you?

Second, the parts that pull. Your part (a) sets "perfect" as the standard and you fault T for falling short of it on classical systems. But for ideal closed quantum systems you promise only "arbitrarily high but not perfect accuracy." Meanwhile (1.2) is presented as an empirical principle with the same standing as the laws of thermodynamics, while its load-bearing premise (d) is — on your own concession — fixed and uncheckable. Which gives way: the word "perfect," or the claim that (1.2) is empirical? Where is the line drawn, and what would show the line is in the wrong place?
transcript.author:
**Patches.** It just states the limit. The proof needs finiteness — openness plus finite convex combination in a finite-dimensional J — and stops there. My explanation says nothing about why Nature should differ outside the line; I drew it where the proof ran out. That's a fact about the proof, not the world. Stated, not held.

The superselection exclusion is a patch made in advance — "we lose no generality by excluding" is assertion, not derivation. If it's swallowing a job, here's the reading that would worry me: a system whose accessible space is a disjoint union of sectors with no possible interference between them, so its realizable dynamics sit *on* the boundary of G, not in the open interior. Then (3.12)'s left inequality becomes an equality for real systems, openness fails, and convex combination has no interior to fill. That would show I excluded the sector that mattered.

**Which gives way.** You've cornered the seam. For closed ideal systems I promise approximation, not perfection — so "perfect" survives only because I've narrowed the domain to *realizable* systems, which (d) says are mixed and dissipative. But narrowing the domain to save the word is precisely what I fault T for — T approximates continuous systems, I called that not perfect. Concede: I've drawn the line at the same place. And (d), which does the narrowing, is fixed and uncheckable. So (1.2) earns "empirical" only in the framework sense I gave for thermodynamics — indirectly falsifiable via the theories it frames. If pure states proved realizable, both "perfect" and the empiricity collapse together. Where would I read the line misdrawn? There: non-unitary, non-(3.8) dynamics, or a finite system Q cannot simulate.

report:
# Report: Deutsch (1985), "Quantum theory, the Church–Turing principle and the universal quantum computer"

## 1. The question, frozen
**What is being explained:** whether quantum theory is *compatible* with the strong physical Church–Turing principle (1.2) — "every finitely realizable physical system can be perfectly simulated by a universal model computing machine operating by finite means." **Range:** finite-dimensional state spaces, no superselection sectors, realizable (mixed, dissipative) systems. The cosmological claim — "does (1.2) hold in Nature?" — is a separate claim, which the author says stays open. **Kind of question:** forward — what permits the match — carried as a consistency question. **The contrast that could have gone otherwise:** a finitely realizable system whose dynamics are *not* the projection of unitary evolution in a larger space, or with no finite bound on distinguishable states. Watched for at two places the author names: whether the realizable set G is genuinely open in J, and the linearity test.

## 2. The parts, in the author's words
(a) perfect simulation, set as a black-box functional match under labellings; (b) the "finite means" conditions (i)–(iii); (c) the third law (1.3); (d) no realizable system can be prepared in a pure, uncorrelated state; (e) density matrices and the superscattering matrix $; (f) G is an open set in J; (g) the dense-subset-plus-finite-convex-combination finish. Also: the §2 universality theorem, the §3 running-time bound, the Bekenstein bound, and the Everett "intolerable strain" claim.

## 3. Part by part

| Part | Mark | Why |
|---|---|---|
| (a) perfect simulation | **Held** | It fixes the standard of success, and the black-box form avoids triviality. |
| (b) finite means (i)–(iii) | **Idle** for this question | Guards against cheating, but does no discriminating work here: both T and Q satisfy (i)–(iii). |
| (c) third law (1.3) | **Idle** | The author names it as the label hung on (d); its work is (d)'s. |
| (d) no pure, uncorrelated realizable state | **Fixed** | The author set it, from (1.3). Asked what change would show it false, he concedes: none. Uncheckable, and load-bearing. |
| (e) density matrices + $ | **Idle** in part | More index structure than the proof uses; the proof needs only that the realizable set is convex and non-extremal. |
| (f) G open in J | **Held if** | Held only by (d) — itself fixed — and by the premise that arbitrary couplings occur (no superselection), also fixed. |
| (g) dense subset + convex combination | **Held** | By (f). |
| §2 universality theorem | **Built** | Worked out by induction with the thing in view; a burden independent of (d). |
| §3 running-time bound N²−2N+2 | **Unknown** | A conjecture; best attained only at N=2. Three tests named would settle it. |
| Bekenstein bound (3.15) | **Borrowed** | Rests on black-hole thermodynamics, conditionally. |
| Everett "intolerable strain" | **Borrowed** | The theorem's predictions do not move between Everett and Copenhagen; held by a separate explanation. |
| finite-dimensional cut | **Fixed** | Drawn after, where the proof ran out — a fact about the proof, not about Nature. |
| superselection exclusion | **Fixed** | "We lose no generality by excluding" is assertion, not derivation. |

Never add these up.

## 4. Whole-explanation checks
**Flip.** Had Q failed to simulate some finite system, the author names what we would see: non-unitary, non-(3.8) dynamics, or a finite system Q cannot simulate. So the outer claim is exposed. Flip (d): if pure states were preparable, G stops being open, and the finish fails on the boundary — the theorem's live joint.

**Direction.** Forward, from (d) and no-superselection, through openness, to the finish. Not run backwards from outputs.

**Answer hidden in the starting points.** This is the sharpest worry, and the author grants it. (d) does the narrowing that lets the word "perfect" survive — saving it by restricting the domain to realizable, mixed systems, which is exactly the move he faults T for making.

**Where the jobs came from.** The range and the jobs were set by the author: finite-dimensional, no superselection, "realizable" = mixed. The fit proves less than it looks.

**Pairs that pull.** (a)'s "perfect" against the mere "arbitrarily high but not perfect accuracy" promised for closed systems; and (1.2)'s "empirical" standing against (d)'s uncheckability. Which gives way? The author conceded the whole seam: "perfect" survives only by the domain-narrowing that (d) supplies, and (d) is fixed. Both collapse together if a pure state is ever realizable.

**Catch-alls and gauges.** The superselection exclusion is a patch made in advance; the author now supplies a gauge — a system whose dynamics sit on the boundary, with disjoint, non-interfering sectors. The finite-dimensional cut has no gauge: nothing inside says why the world should differ outside the line.

**What the change list leaves out.** Infinite-dimensional state spaces (quantum field theory), superselection sectors, cosmology. Left out now openly; the finite-dimension limit was drawn after looking.

**Rival.** A classical stochastic machine matches every marginal (3.2) but cannot match Q's joint correlations (3.3)–(3.6); separated by locality, read off in the joint statistics, not the bits. And because perfect simulation is behavioural, any machine with the same superscattering matrix satisfies (1.2) — the theorem does not pin the workings.

**Where the parts came from.** Built: the §2 theorem. Fixed: (d), the range, the superselection cut. Borrowed: Bekenstein, Everett. Asserted/unknown: the running-time bound.

## 5. What would make it harder to vary
Give (d) a gauge: name a realizable system that would come out on the boundary — the author's own candidate is genuine information loss in black-hole evaporation. That turns (d) from fixed to held-if and exposes the theorem at its one live joint. Second, state the approximation error for closed systems and how it grows, so "perfect" is not rescued by narrowing the domain.

## 6. What this does not show
Hard to vary is not the same as true. Passing shows the compatibility claim is exposed at (d) and that its range is now stated — not that (1.2) holds in Nature. No score is implied.

## 7. One next step
Measure the (d) gauge: run the black-hole information-loss question as the test of whether the realizable set is open at the point the proof needs.
